| Field | |
|---|---|
| **Year** | 2022 |
| **Models** | **Mouse only** in the demonstration: two independent mouse brain datasets. The pipeline itself is built for any species |
| **Brain region** | Not matched between the two datasets: **medial prefrontal cortex** in one, **dentate gyrus of the hippocampus** in the other |
| **Measures** | **RNA** |
| **Method** | Bulk RNA-seq, reprocessed from raw reads. **De novo assembly** with Trinity, no reference genome. Quantification with RSEM, normalised to TPM, with TMM as an option |
| **Cross-species stats** | Orthology by **OrthoMCL**: all-versus-all BLAST of predicted proteins, then Markov clustering into **orthologous gene groups**. Expression compared per group |

## My reading

Now I am reading this paper, which is called **the comparative transcriptomics analysis
pipeline for the meta-analysis of phylogenetically divergent datasets**, which is an amazing
project. It encounters all the problems we had, specifically with **orthologues** and how
orthologues differ from species to species, and also the **RNA sequencing datasets** have been
taken into consideration in terms of data divergence.

This pipeline aims at retrieving gene expression data from **any RNA sequencing dataset**
using **de novo assembly**, **standardized gene expression tools**, and the implementation of
**OrthoMCL**, in order to allow for faster and more statistically, or bioinformatically, clean
datasets. It is a much clearer approach. They have demonstrated this project on **two mouse
brain transcriptomes**.

The background for this project was that **transcriptional regulation** is an important player
for certain diseases, and also for certain gene expression between different species. The
issue with all of that is that transcriptomic divergences between groups are **time consuming
for researchers to understand**, and even more so how to categorize, for instance, different
orthologues. So that is the issue we had: we were not sure how to categorize orthologues and
how to use their gene expression levels accordingly.

They are solving this issue by introducing **CoRMAP**. It **processes raw datasets in the same
way for each species**. OrthoMCL creates **orthologous groups** and allows for gene expression
analysis in relation to the different orthologous groups.

That is where I am currently at. I will continue reading.

**The workflow figure.** I have come across their figure, which explains CoRMAP in a better
way. The first thing that happens in this pipeline is to:

1. **Download the RNA sequencing raw data** from public repositories.
2. **Clean the data.**
3. Do **de novo assembly**.
4. **Quantify** all gene expression values. I assume it is something that we can input.
5. **Predict the protein sequences.**
6. **Find orthologous relationships** between species and/or taxonomic groups with the
   **OrthoMCL pipeline**, which is not elaborated in this figure.
7. **Annotate the mammalian sequences as representative**, using **BLASTP, BLASTX and
   Trinotate**.
8. **Report a metadata table.**
9. Allow for the **downstream analysis with the OGG analysis**, which I think they have also
   published, so this tool also belongs to them.

## What I take from it

An amazing project, and a much clearer approach. It encounters all the problems we had,
specifically with orthologues and how to use their gene expression levels.

## Checks against the paper

- **Is this the same orthologue categorisation problem?** Yes. CoRMAP does not choose between
  one-to-one and one-to-many: OrthoMCL clusters orthologues and in-paralogues into orthologous
  gene groups, and expression is compared per group.
- **Is quantification something that can be input?** It is done by the pipeline: reads are
  mapped back to the assembly and quantified with RSEM inside Trinity, then normalised to TPM.
  The input is raw RNA sequencing data, either public or one's own.
- **Is the OGG analysis their own published tool?** The OGG analysis is part of CoRMAP itself,
  written as their own R scripts. OrthoMCL, Trinity and Trinotate are existing tools by others.
